reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Denotes clustering of multiple autoimmune endocrine failures in one patient, with type 1 and type 2 differing in genetics, age of onset, and component diseases
Type 1 (APECED) is a monogenic disorder of childhood defined by chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene
Type 2 is the more common, polygenic, HLA-associated adult form, typically combining adrenal insufficiency with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes
Because component disorders emerge over years, diagnosis of one autoimmune endocrinopathy should prompt vigilance and periodic screening for others
Adrenal insufficiency is the most dangerous component and may be unmasked or worsened when thyroid hormone is started without glucocorticoid cover
Non-endocrine autoimmune conditions frequently coexist, including vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, and alopecia
Autoantibody testing and periodic biochemical surveillance guide early detection of evolving gland failure
Management is replacement of each failed hormone, with careful sequencing and stress dosing of glucocorticoids
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune polyglandular syndromes result from immune-mediated destruction of multiple endocrine glands and other tissues. In type 1, loss-of-function mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene impair thymic negative selection of self-reactive T cells, allowing autoimmunity against several organs from early life. In type 2, susceptibility is polygenic and strongly linked to HLA haplotypes and other immune-regulatory loci, producing autoimmune attack on the adrenal cortex, thyroid, and pancreatic islets among others. Circulating organ-specific autoantibodies mark the affected tissues, and gland failure becomes clinically apparent once functional reserve is exhausted, which is why components appear sequentially rather than simultaneously.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated autoimmune endocrine disease (e.g. solitary Addison disease or Hashimoto thyroiditis)
Non-autoimmune causes of the individual gland failures
IPEX syndrome and other monogenic immune dysregulation disorders
Multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes (functionally distinct but multiglandular)
Iatrogenic multi-gland dysfunction (e.g. checkpoint inhibitor endocrinopathies)
DiGeorge syndrome for hypoparathyroidism with immune features
additionalInvestigations: Morning cortisol and ACTH with dynamic adrenal testing to detect adrenal insufficiency
Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies
Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and islet autoantibodies
Calcium, phosphate, and PTH for hypoparathyroidism (particularly type 1)
Vitamin B12, coeliac serology, and other autoantibody panels as indicated
Genetic testing for AIRE mutations when type 1 is suspected
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hyponatraemia, and collapse requiring emergency treatment
Precipitation of adrenal crisis by initiating thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid replacement
Severe hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism causing tetany or seizures
Invasive candidiasis or intercurrent illness destabilising multiple hormone axes
reference.prognosis: With early detection and lifelong replacement of each affected hormone, patients can do well, but the risk of undiagnosed adrenal insufficiency and the progressive addition of new autoimmune diseases necessitate ongoing surveillance; type 1 tends to be more severe with a broader disease spectrum.
pitfalls: Treating a single endocrinopathy without screening for others in the syndrome
Starting levothyroxine before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency
Failing to educate patients on glucocorticoid stress dosing
Overlooking non-endocrine autoimmune components such as coeliac disease or pernicious anaemia
Not offering genetic counselling and family screening in type 1 disease
management: Lifelong replacement of each failed hormone axis: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid for adrenal insufficiency, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, insulin for type 1 diabetes and calcium with an activated vitamin D analogue for hypoparathyroidism
Always establish and treat adrenal insufficiency before commencing thyroxine, as thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis
Management of associated non-endocrine autoimmunity, including antifungals for chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and treatment of coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia
Patient education in sick-day rules, provision of a steroid emergency card and injectable hydrocortisone for intercurrent illness
Emergency treatment of adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation
Periodic biochemical and autoantibody surveillance for the sequential emergence of additional gland failures
Endocrinology-led multidisciplinary care with genetic counselling and family screening where the monogenic AIRE-driven type 1 form is identified
